domain: Maritime pilotage — compulsory harbour and river pilotage: berth-to-berth passage planning, the master-pilot exchange card, the pilot-ladder transfer, conduct-of-navigation ('the con') versus command, under-keel clearance and squat allowance, fixed abort points and the last point of no return, and the bridge-team duty to challenge a conning order
axioms: The party taking conduct never receives the whole picture: local knowledge is largely undocumented, so every handoff is lossy by construction and the design question is which losses are detectable by the receiver rather than how to eliminate them.

A plan is a statement about conditions at the moment it was written; unless it pins those conditions, the receiver cannot tell a still-valid plan from a stale one, and a stale plan executes just as smoothly as a sound one.

Conduct transfers but responsibility does not: the party that wrote the plan remains accountable for it, which means the executor's duty on encountering a defect is to report and stop, and the design must say what stopping leaves behind.

Casualties cluster at the transfer itself — the ladder, not the channel — so the spawn boundary (environment, cwd, permissions, tool access, model pin, tree state) deserves more scrutiny than either role's steady-state behaviour.
Every passage needs a named abort point and a safe state reachable from it; a process that can only complete or fail leaves the vessel stopped in the channel.
Margins are allowances, not estimates: a context budget without a stated reserve is an assumption that will be discovered only when it is already exceeded.
Silent divergence between plan and world is the characteristic killer; loud failure is survivable because it recruits the party who still holds the picture.
primitives: exchange card (what the plan file carries across the boundary)
undocumented local knowledge (session context the orchestrator holds and cannot transfer)
passage plan preconditions (commit SHA, clean tree, branch identity, dependency versions)
transfer moment (the spawn: env, cwd, worktree, permissions, tools, model resolution)
the con vs. command (executor scope authority vs. orchestrator responsibility)
challenge duty (whether the executor may or must dispute a plan order)
abort point and safe state (what a returned item leaves behind)
under-keel clearance / squat allowance (context budget and its reserve)
set and drift (repo state moving beneath a written plan)
passage report (the executor's return format and its size)
relieving the pilot (two-strikes escalation back to the orchestrator)
failure_mode: Sees only the joints: takes the three roles, the model assignment, and the economics as given, so it cannot argue that the whole shape is unnecessary or that a different decomposition would be cheaper.

Structurally conservative about handoffs — will recommend more preconditions, assertions, and fixed formats, and systematically under-weights the cost of the ceremony it adds; has no way to notice that a plan template heavy enough to satisfy it would push work back into the orchestrator's context and defeat the gate.

Blind to whether a check is worth running at all: it treats verification as an event at the boundary, not as evidence, so it cannot assess validator value, independence of criteria, or whether PASS means anything.
No vocabulary for cost, pricing, cache economics, or token accounting, so any finding about the gate's arithmetic or the pool's weighting is invisible to it.
Assumes an in-motion process with a single continuous item; poorly equipped for questions about batching, parallelism across many items, or which item classes should route to a different lane.
Over-indexes on the rare catastrophic transfer and may inflate the severity of losses that in practice recruit a loud, cheap retry.
